questions.question: Which of the following best defines a system bus in a microcomputer?

options.A: A single line that carries power to the CPU.
options.B: A collection of separate lines that connect CPU, memory, and I/O modules.
options.C: The memory chip that stores program instructions.
options.D: An external peripheral used for data storage.

questions.explanation:
A system bus is described as “the bus that connects major microcomputer components such as CPU, memory or I/O” and consists of multiple separate lines [Page 42].

---

questions.question: What does the width of a data bus (e.g., 8, 16, 32, 64) indicate?

options.A: The number of devices that can be attached to the bus.
options.B: The voltage level used for signaling.
options.C: The number of bits transferred simultaneously on the bus.
options.D: The maximum clock frequency of the system.

questions.explanation:
The width “represents the number of bits they can carry because each carries 1 bit” [Page 42].

---

questions.question: In the bus control signals, what condition does a low LOCK signal represent?

options.B: Other bus masters are allowed to take control.
options.C: Other bus masters are prevented from gaining the bus.

questions.explanation:
The LOCK output “indicates that other system bus master will be prevented from gaining the system bus, while the LOCK signal is low” [Page 42].

---

questions.question: The pins RQ/GT0 and RQ/GT1 are used for which purpose?

options.A: To select the data bus width.
options.B: To request and grant bus control between local bus masters.
options.C: To reset the CPU after power‑up.

questions.explanation:
RQ/GT0, RQ/GT1 “are used by the other local bus master… to force the processor to release the local bus” [Page 42].

---

questions.question: Which three groups of lines typically compose a system bus?
questions.explanation:
The text states that “in any system bus the lines can be classified into three group buses,” which are understood to be address, data, and control lines [Page 42].

---

questions.question: If a data bus is 32 bits wide, how many bits can be transferred in a single bus cycle?
questions.explanation:
The bus width directly equals the number of bits transferred per cycle; a 32‑bit bus carries 32 bits [Page 42].

---

questions.question: A microcomputer uses an 8‑bit data bus. How many whole bytes can be moved across the bus in one cycle?
questions.explanation:
8 bits equal 1 byte, so an 8‑bit bus transfers one byte per cycle [Page 42].

---

questions.question: Assuming the address bus has 16 lines and the data bus is 8 bits wide, what is the maximum addressable memory size?
questions.explanation:
A 16‑line address bus can select 2¹⁶ = 65 536 locations; with an 8‑bit (1‑byte) data width, this yields 65 536 bytes = 64 KB [Page 42].

---

questions.question: During a synchronous read operation, which signal is used to confirm that the data on the data bus is valid?
questions.explanation:
The synchronous read description lists “Acknowledge Signal” as one of the lines involved in the operation [Page 43].

---

questions.question: In an asynchronous read operation, which two synchronization signals are explicitly mentioned?
questions.explanation: The asynchronous read description includes “MSYNC” and “SSYNC” among the signals used [Page 44].
